newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Hutu exodus offers hope, but crisis not over.
newsitem.headline: Hutu exodus offers hope, but crisis not over.

text.p: The return of thousands of Hutu refugees to Rwanda has given the world its first glimmer of hope in Zaire's refugee crisis.
But with many more scattered across eastern Zaire and fresh fighting there, the crisis brought to a head by last month's revolt by Tutsi and other Zairean rebels looks far from solved.
The exodus began with the departure from amongst the refugees' midst of militiamen who had previously prevented them from going home.

The refugees had been held virtual hostage in the huge Mugunga camp, intimidated into staying in exile, until Zairean rebels bombarded it on Thursday ahead of the planned arrival of a multinational force.
The Hutu militiamen, blamed for the 1994 genocide of some 800,000 mostly Tutsi people in Rwanda, were reported to have fled into the bush.
As many as 700,000 Hutus, previously crowded into the world's largest refugee camp, joined the march.
The unexpected exodus came ahead of Friday's U.N. Security Council decision to give legitimacy to a multinational force to aid 1.2 million Hutu refugees and many displaced Zaireans.
"The impasse has been broken," Ray Wilkinson of the U.N. refugee agency (UNHCR) said. "This is amazing and unstoppable."
The refugees abandoned the debris of two years of exile and the freshly mutilated bodies of several dozen men, women and children -- deaths some blamed on rebels.
Further west and deeper in Zaire, witnesses reported fighting between Zairean rebels and fleeing Hutu hardliners.

Over a million Hutus fled Rwanda fearing reprisals after the 1994 genocide and a civil war in which an army dominated by returning Tutsi exiles took power. Hundreds of thousands of Hutus fled from an equally bitter civil war in Burundi.
The revolt in the east, which groups ethnic Tutsis from Zaire and other opponents of ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, has also put hundreds of thousands of Zaireans to flight.
Heavy rain halted Friday's exodus after nightfall. Hoards of refugees huddled at the roadside under plastic sheeting.
But with the armed Hutu hardliners moving west, a regrouping of Hutu refugees further inside Zaire remains likely. Logistical problems of dealing with the Hutu influx to Rwanda are huge.

With the whereabouts of many who earlier fled deeper into Zaire remains unclear, the World Health Organisation confirmed an outbreak of cholera among Zaireans in Sake. Earlier, doctors spoke of cholera among 250,000 refugees near Mwenga in the east.

Rwanda's Hutu president Pasteur Bizimungu was at the border to welcome returnees. "We have come here to welcome the people to show them the whole population was waiting for them to reassure them there won't be any harassment," he said.
In the light of the exodus, Rwanda questioned the need for the planned 10,000-strong, Canadian-led multinational force but the U.N. said there remained plenty of work for it to do.

"Everybody is absolutely elated, but we still desperately need the multinational force," U.N. spokesman Sylvana Foa said. "We have stocks in Rwanda for about 450,000 people, but we are going to need a lot of help to move these people around."
Zaire says it wants a say on the composition of the force and opposes creation of new refugee camps on its territory. It wants corridors to facilitate the return home of refugees.
"There is no place for any Rwandan refugee in Zaire whoever it is," Information Minister Boguo Makeli said.
But the crisis has bred new and deep-seated bitterness.

Zairean deputy Foreign Minister Lokondo Yoka, speaking in Brussels, accused Rwanda and Burundi's Tutsi-dominated armies of occupying the eastern towns of Uvira, Bukavu and Goma. "We are determined to wage a total war... We have the means," he said.
